structure.title: Household and citizenship
structure.text: Early books examine the household, proposed ideal arrangements, and the question of who counts as a citizen.

structure.title: Constitutions and education
structure.text: Later books compare regimes, causes of instability, and the education appropriate to a political community.

people.name: Polis
people.text: For Aristotle, the city-state is the community in which human beings live not merely to survive but to live well, and the book asks what makes one good.

people.name: Citizen
people.text: A citizen, in his definition, is someone who takes part in judging and holding office, which makes the question of who counts as one a central political dispute.

people.name: Constitution
people.text: The way a city distributes power among the one, the few and the many; Aristotle compares many of them, real and proposed, to ask which works best.

context.title: A restricted citizen body
context.text: Aristotle's account excludes many inhabitants and defends hierarchies that require criticism. Its language of shared life does not include everyone equally.
context.takeaway: Ask who is left outside each definition.

context.title: Practical comparison
context.text: The inquiry moves between desirable arrangements and what particular cities can sustain. The best imaginable regime is not always the immediate question.

notice.why: Groups can elevate their advantage into a general principle.

notice.text: Notice the connection between education and regime.
notice.why: Constitutions depend on habits as well as laws.

opening: The rich say their property entitles them to rule; the poor say their numbers do. Both can make a claim about justice, and both have reasons to confuse the city's good with their own advantage. Aristotle examines constitutions as arrangements made by people who want different things from living together. His investigation includes arguments about slavery and exclusion that demand resistance, alongside a persistent practical question: how can a community govern itself without letting one group's victory become everybody else's insecurity?
